title: Aprapransa
author: Kwesi Arkoh
desc: Toasted corn meal stirred into palm nut soup with crab until it goes pasty — and the cue is that the fresh taste of the palm has completely gone.
longDesc: Aprapransa is palm nut soup thickened into a one-pot with toasted corn meal, which makes it a swallow and a soup at once. Eight ladles of soup go into a separate pan, the palm nut extract is diluted with warm water and boiled, strained onto the meat, crab added after five minutes and cooked fifteen to twenty-five minutes, then nine to ten tablespoons of corn meal are stirred in gradually until pasty. The doneness cue is specific and good: the palm oil separates to the top, and you taste to check that the fresh taste of the palm is completely gone. Which community it belongs to is genuinely unsettled.
ingredients: Warm water, for diluting the palm nut extract
steps: Scoop 8 ladles of palm nut soup into a separate pan.
Dilute the palm nut extract with warm water and bring to the boil.
Add the roasted cornmeal gradually, stirring continuously, until the mixture is pasty.
Check the cue: the palm oil should separate to the top, and the fresh taste of the palm should be completely gone.
Garnish with tomato stew and serve.
chefTips: The doneness cue is the best thing about this recipe and it has two halves: palm oil separating to the top, AND tasting to confirm the fresh taste of the palm is completely gone. Raw palm flavour is the fault this dish fails on.
Gradually, stirring continuously, for the cornmeal. Dumped in, it seizes into lumps you cannot break.
Toasted corn meal, which is tom brown — not raw cornmeal. The toasting is what gives the dish its nutty depth.
Crab in after five minutes, not at the start. It needs the shorter cook.
Nine to ten tablespoons to eight ladles is the only published ratio. Eight ladles is not a precise measure, so judge by the paste rather than the spoon count.
The tomato stew garnish is traditional rather than decorative — it sits on top and is stirred through as you eat.

Which people this dish belongs to is not settled. One broadcaster says GaDangme; Osseo-Asare first met it in the Eastern Region under its Twi name and records apragyaa as the Fante name; a news agency presents Apregyae as Fante festival food. All three are recorded.
commonMistakes: Adding the cornmeal all at once.
Using raw rather than toasted cornmeal.
Stopping before the palm oil separates, leaving a raw palm taste.
Crab in from the beginning, so it overcooks.
sources: Quantities and method adapted from 'Recipes: How to prepare Aprapransa using palm nut soup', GhanaWeb, 2 June 2017. SOURCING FLAG, stated plainly: the page carries NO BYLINE and credits 'recipes.ghanaculturepolitics.com'. It therefore fails the named-author bar beyond the named publisher, and is used only because it is the sole source consulted that publishes any quantities at all for this dish. Everything taken from it is flagged as coming from an unbylined page.
Quantities exactly as printed: 'Scoop 8 ladles' of soup into a separate pan; '9-10 tablespoons cornmeal'; 'serves 3 people'.
Method as printed: dilute the palm nut extract with warm water and boil; strain into the meat; add crab 'after 5 minutes'; cook 15-25 minutes; add the cornmeal gradually while stirring until 'pasty'.

THE DONENESS CUE, verbatim, and the reason this entry is publishable at all: 'Palm oil separates to the top. Also, taste to see if the fresh taste of the palm is completely gone.' That is a genuine two-part observable endpoint and it is quoted rather than paraphrased.

THE COMMUNITY QUESTION IS NOT SETTLED, and three named sources disagree. (1) Dankwa Prince, 'Ghana Month: Apapransa…', Ghana Broadcasting Corporation, 26 March 2024: the dish 'originates with the GaDangme people'. (2) Fran Osseo-Asare and Barbara Baëta, The Ghana Cookbook (Hippocrene, 2015), in the headnote to 'Toasted Cornmeal One-Pot with Crab', verbatim: 'This dish has several names. I first met it in the Eastern Region as its Twi name, Aprapransa. It is also called akpledzi (Ga or Ewe), apragyaa (Fante), or akplijii.' (3) Isaac Arkoh, 'Celebrating Oguaa Fetu Afahye with sumptuous Fanti delicacies', Ghana News Agency, 1 September 2023, presents 'Apregyae' as Fante festival food: 'palmnut soup and powdered roasted corn (tom brown), well spiced with salted fish' with crabs and a tomato stew garnish, eaten with rice, jollof or waakye. The community field above records the dispute rather than picking one.

THE GHANA COOKBOOK entry for this dish is the best-credentialed source in existence for it — 6 servings, medium difficulty — but its QUANTITIES AND METHOD WERE NOT OBTAINABLE. The publisher's platform shows only headnotes and yields. That is why an unbylined page is carrying this recipe, and it is a real gap rather than a preference.
The Ghana News Agency piece is also the source for the tom brown identification and the tomato stew garnish, both of which corroborate the unbylined recipe's method independently.
storage: 2 days refrigerated. It sets very firm.
reheating: Low heat with water or extra soup stirred in to loosen.
healthBenefits: Crab is high in protein, selenium and vitamin B12 and very low in fat.
Red palm oil supplies provitamin-A carotenoids.
Toasted maize provides fibre and B vitamins.
A complete one-pot meal with starch, protein and fat in one bowl.
culturalNote: Aprapransa turns up at Fante festivals, in Ga households and under a Twi name in the Eastern Region, which is probably the honest answer to who it belongs to — a coastal dish that travelled and got renamed at every stop. The list of its names in The Ghana Cookbook is the clearest evidence of that: four names for one pot of toasted corn, palm nut soup and crab.
